subtitle: Apply the culture lens to access: how worship of the written word, only one right way and perfectionism can build barriers into DSD work, and how plain language, alternative formats, Universal Design, disability justice and collective access can take them out.
audience: For DHS and DSD staff, supervisors, managers, trainers and policy and communications staff who write for the public, design processes or trainings, plan meetings and engagement, or support colleagues who may need accommodations.

lessons.title: Worship of the written word and accessible communication
objectives: Explain how the characteristic Okun calls worship of the written word can become an access barrier in public service.
Describe the ADA Title II effective communication requirement and examples of auxiliary aids and alternative formats.
Apply the DHS content guidelines on plain language to a public-facing document.
Design more than one route for input that is documented and given equal weight in the record.
lessons.teaching:
Module 3 introduced Tema Okun's framework as a lens on the norms an institution treats as neutral. One of those norms, which Okun calls worship of the written word, describes a culture in which knowledge counts only when it arrives in writing, usually in a particular formal style. Public service depends on writing. Notices, plans, bulletins and records protect due process and accountability, and Okun has distinguished sound writing from this characteristic. The access concern is narrower: when dense written English becomes the only route in or out of a process. A long PDF notice, a written-only comment period, a request that must be submitted on a detailed form, or a meeting where only the person who drafted the memo is heard can each screen out people who have relevant knowledge and every right to take part.

Some of the floor here is set by law. The ADA.gov guidance on effective communication explains that state and local governments, including DHS, must provide auxiliary aids and services when needed so that communication with people who have vision, hearing or speech disabilities is as effective as communication with others. Examples include large print, Braille, electronic documents that work with screen-reading software, qualified sign language and other interpreters, and real-time captioning. The agency must give primary consideration to the aid the person asks for and honor that choice unless another equally effective method is available or the request would cause a fundamental alteration or an undue burden. Even then, it must provide an effective alternative, and an undue burden decision must come from an official no lower than a department head, with written reasons.

Plain language is the everyday tool for the same goal. The DHS content guidelines ask writers to write so people can understand the information on the first read, to write for the people who need it and what they need to know or do, and to aim for a fifth- to sixth-grade reading level when the subject allows. The guidelines also caution that reading level alone does not make content clear; structure, headings and familiar terms matter too. Plain language is not simplifying the substance. It is precision about what the reader needs, and the best test is to try a draft with the people who will use it, such as self-advocates, family members or lead agency staff, before it goes out.

The culture question sits underneath the rules. When a comment arrives as a phone call, an interpreted conversation, a video in American Sign Language or a few words spoken at a listening session, does it carry the same weight in the record as a polished written submission? A team can keep the record and widen the routes into it: offer a plain-language summary and accessible formats alongside the full document, accept spoken and interpreted input, write it down accurately, and show how it was considered. The Accessibility domain of this pathway asks who a process is designed for. Writing that only some readers can use answers that question without anyone saying so.
lessons.keyPoint: Keep the written record and widen the routes into it. Effective communication sets a legal floor; plain language, accessible formats and documented spoken input help make sure knowledge counts whatever form it arrives in.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD team is gathering public input on a proposed change to how people request a change in their service plan. The only route is a long online written form open for thirty days. {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}}, who works with a self-advocacy group, tells the team that several members want to comment but find the form hard to read and would rather talk through their views. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} worries that spoken comments will be harder to document and compare with written ones.
lessons.question: What is the strongest way for the team to respond?
choices: Keep the written form as the official route and offer staff help filling it out for anyone who asks.
Add a plain-language summary and accessible formats, accept spoken and interpreted comments with accurate notes, and treat all routes the same when reviewing input.
Extend the comment period by two weeks so people have more time to complete the form.
feedback: Help with the form is useful, but it keeps one route as the real one and makes people ask for assistance to be heard. Their knowledge still has to pass through a format that does not fit them.

This keeps a reliable record while widening the ways in. Documenting spoken input carefully answers the program manager's concern, and equal treatment in review means the change is real rather than symbolic.
More time can help, but it does not address the barrier the partner described. A dense form is still dense after six weeks.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider a document or process in your work where writing is the only route. Who might have knowledge that never reaches you because of it? You may use the practice case instead.
lessons.action: Choose one public-facing document your team owns. Check it against the DHS content guidelines, note which alternative formats are available and how a person would request one, and identify one non-written route for questions or input that could be documented.

check.question: Under the ADA Title II effective communication rules, what must an agency give primary consideration to?
check.correct: The auxiliary aid or service the person with a disability asks for.
wrong: Whichever format is least expensive for the agency to produce.
The format most staff are already comfortable using.
check.feedback: The agency must honor the person's choice unless another equally effective method is available or the request would cause a fundamental alteration or undue burden, and it must still provide an effective alternative.

lessons.title: Only one right way: flexibility, Universal Design and UDL
objectives: Explain how the characteristic Okun calls only one right way can turn a standard method into an access barrier.
Separate the goal a standard protects from the method used to meet it.
Describe the principles of Universal Design and the three Universal Design for Learning principles.
Redesign a process or training so that flexibility is offered by default rather than only on request.
lessons.teaching:
Another characteristic on Okun's list is the belief that there is only one right way to do something, and that people who do it differently need to be corrected. In access terms, this often shows up as a single format: one way to attend a meeting, one way to complete a training, one way to show competence, one route to make a request. Public agencies have good reasons to standardize. Consistent processes help make sure similar cases are treated alike, and that is a fairness value. The Cultural Tensions reframing from Module 3 names this pair directly: standardization and accessibility. The useful question is whether a standard is about the goal or about the method. Accurate documentation may be essential; the requirement that it be typed at a desk in one sitting may not be.

Universal Design offers a way to build flexibility in from the start. The Center for Universal Design at North Carolina State University, in its 1997 principles, defined it as the design of products and environments to be usable by all people, to the greatest extent possible, without the need for adaptation or specialized design. Its seven principles are equitable use, flexibility in use, simple and intuitive use, perceptible information, tolerance for error, low physical effort, and size and space for approach and use. They were written for products and buildings, and their authors noted that they address usability only and that not every principle applies to every design. Many DSD processes, from forms to meetings, can still be tested against them. Does the request process tolerate an error without starting over? Is the key information perceptible to someone who cannot see the screen?

Universal Design for Learning applies the same thinking to training and learning. CAST's UDL Guidelines, version 3.0, released in 2024, organize the approach around three principles: provide multiple means of engagement, multiple means of representation, and multiple means of action and expression. For a DSD training delivered to staff, lead agencies or providers, that might mean a captioned video with a transcript, slides shared ahead in an accessible format, the choice to pause and return, and more than one way to show what someone learned, such as a discussion or a short written response. A standard of understanding can stay the same while the paths to it multiply.

Universal Design does not replace individual accommodation. Some needs are specific to a person, and the formal accommodation and effective communication processes still apply. What design changes is how often people must ask, and how much they must reveal to get what they need. When captions, transcripts, flexible timing and multiple formats are offered to everyone, a person does not have to disclose a disability to use them. That matters for the next lesson, because the cost of asking is often where culture and access meet. A team that offers flexibility by default is also quietly changing a norm about what counts as the right way.
lessons.keyPoint: Separate the goal a standard protects from the method used to meet it. Universal Design and UDL build flexibility in for everyone, which reduces how often people must ask and disclose, without replacing individual accommodation.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} owns a required onboarding module for new DSD staff. It is a forty-five-minute video without a transcript, followed by a quiz that must be completed in one sitting with a perfect score. {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}}, who recently finished it, mentions that it was hard to follow without captions and that the timed quiz measured speed as much as understanding. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} wants to keep the module rigorous.
lessons.question: Which revision best keeps the module rigorous while removing barriers?
choices: Keep the module as it is, since anyone who needs a change can request an accommodation.
Make the module optional so no one is disadvantaged by its format.
Name what the module must teach, add captions and a transcript, allow pausing and returning, remove time limits that are not essential, and keep the knowledge standard.
feedback: Accommodation remains available, but relying on it alone makes each person ask, and often disclose, to get access the design could have offered everyone. The barrier stays in place for the next learner.
Making required content optional lowers the standard instead of removing the barrier. New staff still need what the module teaches.
This separates the goal from the method. Rigor stays where it belongs, in what people learn, while the format stops measuring things the module was never meant to test.
lessons.reflection: Privately think of a standard method in your work that people are expected to follow one way. What goal does it protect, and could the same goal be met another way? You may use the practice case.
lessons.action: Pick one process or training you influence. Write the goal it protects, list the methods currently required, and test the design against two Universal Design principles or the three UDL principles. Identify one flexibility that could be offered to everyone.

check.question: What is the main difference between Universal Design and an individual accommodation?
check.correct: Universal Design builds usability into a process for everyone from the start; an accommodation adjusts for a specific person's need.
wrong: Universal Design replaces the need for any individual accommodation.
Universal Design applies only to buildings, so it has no bearing on forms, meetings or training.
check.feedback: The two work together. Good design reduces how often people need to ask, while the accommodation process remains for needs that design does not meet. The principles can guide forms, meetings and training as well as buildings.

lessons.title: Perfectionism, disclosure and the cost of asking
objectives: Explain how a culture of perfectionism can discourage staff from disclosing a disability or requesting an accommodation.
Describe what State of Minnesota policy says about how accommodation requests are made and who decides them.
Identify supervisor and team practices that lower the cost of asking.
Respond to a work-quality concern without asking about an employee's health.
lessons.teaching:
Okun's list describes perfectionism as a culture where mistakes are treated as reflections of a person's worth, where little time goes to appreciation, and where attention goes mostly to what is wrong. Okun distinguishes this from high standards and excellence, which are not the concern. In the access domain, perfectionism connects to fear and stigma. In a workplace where any visible struggle feels like failure, needing to work differently can feel like admitting a flaw. It is reasonable to expect that some staff will cope quietly rather than ask, especially when a condition is not apparent or changes over time. A request delayed by fear is an access barrier, even if every policy is in place.

The policy itself is designed to make asking simple. Minnesota Management and Budget's Policy 1433 on ADA reasonable accommodations applies to executive branch employees and applicants. A request does not require any special words, and the person does not need to mention the ADA or the word disability. It can be made orally, in writing, electronically or in person, and an oral request is documented in writing. Supervisors must not ask an applicant or employee for medical information. They must promptly forward a request to the appropriate decision maker and tell the person who that is, and they can approve certain low-cost items. The agency ADA coordinator decides requests beyond a supervisor's authority, leads the interactive process and must be consulted before any request is denied. Medical information is kept confidential and stored separately from personnel files. This course does not decide accommodation questions; the ADA coordinator and Human Resources do, under that policy.

Culture determines whether people feel able to use the process. Supervisors and teams can lower the cost of asking in ordinary ways. Mention accommodation to everyone, in the same breath as logistics, rather than only to someone who seems to be struggling. Treat errors as information about the work and the process, not as verdicts about a person. Recognize good work specifically and often. When someone asks for something, focus on what would help, not on why they need it. Keep a request separate from performance discussions, and never treat it as a sign that someone is less capable. Colleagues do not need to know why a teammate works a certain way, and a team that is flexible by default asks people to explain themselves less often.

A supervisor may still need to address work quality, and that conversation can be both direct and safe. Describe the specific work issue and what is going well. Ask what would help, including with tools or systems. Remind the employee that anyone can request an accommodation and how. Do not ask whether a health condition is involved. If you think a medical condition may be affecting the work, Policy 1433 directs supervisors to consult the ADA coordinator on how to proceed rather than asking the employee. Disclosure is the employee's choice. Progress here shows up in the work: arrangements set up without long delays, staff who know how to ask, fewer people working around a barrier on their own. It is not measured by tracking who has asked.
lessons.keyPoint: Perfectionism raises the cost of asking. The policy keeps requests simple and confidential; culture decides whether people use it. Lower the cost of asking, keep work conversations about the work, and never ask about health.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{CASE_MANAGER}} has a long record of careful work, but since the unit moved to a new documentation system, several of {{CASE_MANAGER}}'s reports have been missing required details. {{CASE_MANAGER}} has not raised any concern. {{SUPERVISOR}} needs to address the quality issue and has wondered privately whether something else is going on.
lessons.question: How should {{SUPERVISOR}} approach the conversation?
choices: Meet privately, describe the specific gaps and what is going well, ask what would help with the new system, mention that anyone can request an accommodation and how, and consult the ADA coordinator if a medical condition may be involved.
Ask {{CASE_MANAGER}} directly whether a health condition is causing the errors, so the right support can be offered.
Document the errors in a formal note and wait to see whether the pattern continues before saying anything.
feedback: This addresses the work directly and respectfully, opens the door to support without requiring disclosure, and follows the policy's direction to consult the ADA coordinator rather than asking about health.
However well meant, asking about health is something the policy says supervisors must not do. It can also make the employee feel exposed, which is the fear this lesson describes.
Waiting without a conversation lets the problem grow and signals that mistakes are recorded rather than discussed. It also misses the chance to find out whether the new system is the barrier.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider what makes asking for a change in how you work feel easy or hard in your current team. What one norm, if it changed, would make asking easier for others? You may use the practice case.
lessons.action: Write one sentence you could add to routine meeting invitations, onboarding or project kickoffs that offers accommodation to everyone and says how to ask. Confirm the contact information with Human Resources or the ADA coordinator before using it.

check.question: Under Minnesota Management and Budget Policy 1433, what does an employee need to say to make an accommodation request?
check.correct: No special words; the employee does not need to mention the ADA or the word disability, and the request can be made orally.
wrong: The request must be in writing, on the agency form, and must cite the ADA.
The employee must first provide a diagnosis to the supervisor.
check.feedback: The policy keeps the request simple. Oral requests are documented in writing, supervisors must not ask for medical information, and the ADA coordinator handles documentation when it is needed.

lessons.title: Disability justice and collective access in DSD work
objectives: Describe how disability justice, as Sins Invalid sets it out, differs from and adds to a disability rights approach.
Name the ten principles of disability justice and explain several that bear directly on DSD work.
Plan a meeting or engagement using collective access practices.
Measure access improvements by changes in the work, using a plan, try, study, adjust cycle.
lessons.teaching:
Much of DSD's work rests on disability rights: the ADA, the Olmstead decision and the laws and rules that set what people can expect from public programs. Those rights are a floor that DSD implements. Disability justice, as set out by Sins Invalid, a disability justice arts and movement project, asks a broader question about how ableism connects with other systems of power and what liberation would look like. Sins Invalid describes disability justice as a vision and practice of what is yet to be. Its ten principles are intersectionality, leadership of those most impacted, an anti-capitalist politic, commitment to cross-movement organizing, recognizing wholeness, sustainability, commitment to cross-disability solidarity, interdependence, collective access and collective liberation.

Several principles speak directly to the culture lens in this pathway. Intersectionality reminds us that the same institution can hold racial and ableist defaults at once, so a process that disadvantages disabled people of color may need both lenses to be seen. Leadership of those most impacted asks who shapes a decision, not just who is consulted. Recognizing wholeness, the idea that people have worth beyond economic productivity, connects to the productivity and well-being tension. Sustainability asks for a pace that people and communities can keep. It is also important to be honest about fit. Sins Invalid's principles include an anti-capitalist politic and skepticism that state solutions can deliver liberation. A state agency should not claim the framework as its own or turn it into compliance language. It can learn from it, credit it, and let it challenge how the work is done.

Collective access is the most practical principle for everyday DSD work. Sins Invalid describes it as bringing flexibility and creative nuance that go beyond able-bodied and able-minded norms. In a workplace, it means treating access as a shared responsibility the group plans together, rather than a burden one person carries by asking. For a meeting, that can look like inviting everyone to share access needs in advance without giving reasons, sending materials early in accessible formats, turning on captions, building in breaks, and offering more than one way to participate, such as speaking, using chat or sending thoughts afterward. For community engagement, it means involving self-advocates and families in planning, arranging interpreters and accessible locations, and following agency rules on any compensation for participants' time.

Success should be measured in the work. Useful signs include a notice tested with readers before it went out, alternative formats delivered when they were needed, a barrier removed from a request process, a meeting where participants said they could take part fully, or community input that led to a documented change. Counting how many staff completed a training, or tracking who asked for what, says little about access and can harm privacy. Use a short plan, try, study and adjust cycle. Plan one access change with an owner and a review date. Try it. Study what happened by asking the people affected, and look for any new burden. Adjust, and report back what changed and what did not. Then choose the next barrier.
lessons.keyPoint: Disability rights set a floor; disability justice asks who leads and how access is shared. Collective access makes access the group's responsibility, and progress is measured by barriers removed from the work.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD team is planning community listening sessions about a proposed change to a waiver program. The first plan is two in-person evening sessions in Saint Paul, with slides and written comments accepted for a week afterward. {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}} has agreed to co-plan the sessions. {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} asks what collective access would look like for this plan.
lessons.question: Which revision best reflects collective access?
choices: Add a sign language interpreter to the existing plan and proceed on the current schedule.

Invite self-advocates to help plan, ask every registrant about access needs without asking why, send plain-language materials ahead, offer a captioned virtual option and breaks, document every route for comments, and report back what changed.
Postpone the sessions until a full accessibility audit of all DSD engagement practices is complete.
feedback: An interpreter is an important step, but it treats access as one fix added to a plan designed without the people most affected. Other barriers in the plan, such as location, timing and written-only follow-up, remain.

This shares responsibility for access across the planning group, puts people most affected in a leading role, and gives several documented ways to take part. Reporting back closes the loop and shows whether the effort changed anything.
A broader review may be worthwhile, but postponing delays input the community has a stake in. Collective access can be practiced now and improved through the next cycle.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider a meeting or engagement you have planned or attended. Whose job was access, in practice? What would change if the whole group planned it together? You may use the practice case.
lessons.action: For your next meeting or engagement, use the job aid to plan collective access: an advance access invitation, accessible materials, more than one way to participate, a short check at the end on what worked, and a date to adjust the practice.

check.question: What does collective access mean in a workplace?
check.correct: Access is a shared responsibility the group plans together, rather than a burden one person carries by asking.
wrong: Everyone receives exactly the same format so that no one is treated differently.
Access needs are handled privately by each person so the group's plans do not change.
check.feedback: Collective access shifts the work of access from the individual to the group. It values flexibility, invites needs without requiring reasons, and does not replace the formal accommodation process when it is needed.

cards.front: Worship of the written word (access lens)
cards.back: When writing in one formal style becomes the only route in or out of a process. Keep the record; widen the routes into it.
Under ADA Title II, communication with people with vision, hearing or speech disabilities must be as effective as with others, with primary consideration to the aid the person requests.
Writing so the intended reader can understand and act on the first read. Reading level alone does not make content clear; test drafts with the people who will use them.
Treating a single method as the standard. Separate the goal a standard protects from the method used to meet it.
Design that is usable by as many people as possible without adaptation. UDL applies it to learning through multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression.
How perfectionism, fear and stigma can keep people from requesting an accommodation. Lower it by offering options to everyone and never asking why.
A framework set out by Sins Invalid in ten principles, including intersectionality, leadership of those most impacted, interdependence and collective access.
Access planned as the group's shared responsibility, rather than a burden carried by the person who asks.

aid.heading: Widen the routes, keep the record
items: Check public-facing writing against the DHS content guidelines and test it with intended readers.
Offer accessible formats and say how to request one.
Accept spoken and interpreted input, document it accurately and weigh it the same as written input.

aid.heading: Separate the goal from the method
items: Write the goal a standard protects and list the methods it currently requires.
Test the design against Universal Design principles or the three UDL principles.
Offer at least one flexibility to everyone, such as captions, transcripts or untimed steps.

aid.heading: Lower the cost of asking
items: Offer accommodation to everyone, alongside routine logistics, with a contact.
Keep work conversations about the work; never ask about health or diagnosis.
Forward requests promptly and consult the ADA coordinator when a medical condition may be involved.

aid.heading: Plan collective access
items: Invite people most affected to help plan.
Ask everyone about access needs in advance without requiring reasons.
Provide more than one way to participate, and check at the end what worked.
Measure barriers removed and changes made, not who asked.

sources.title: Tema Okun, White Supremacy Culture: Characteristics (updated 2025)
sources.note: The primary framework for the characteristics used as a lens here, including perfectionism, worship of the written word and only one right way. Okun distinguishes high standards from perfectionism and sound writing from treating written words as the only valid knowledge. It is a practice-based reflection tool, not an empirical instrument, and it does not address disability law.

sources.title: Sins Invalid, 10 Principles of Disability Justice
sources.note: The ten principles as Sins Invalid states them, including collective access and interdependence. It is a movement framework, skeptical of state solutions, not agency guidance; this course draws on it for reflection and credits it rather than adopting it as policy.

sources.title: Cornell University, Principles of Universal Design (NC State Center for Universal Design, 1997)
sources.note: Reproduces the 1997 definition and seven principles of Universal Design. The authors note that the principles address usability only and that not every principle applies to every design; applying them to forms and meetings is this course's suggestion.

sources.title: CAST, Universal Design for Learning Guidelines
sources.note: UDL Guidelines 3.0 (2024), organized around multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression. A design framework for learning, not a legal standard.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget, HR/LR Policy 1433, ADA Reasonable Accommodations
sources.note: Executive branch policy on how requests are made, the roles of supervisors, Human Resources and agency ADA coordinators, and confidentiality of medical information. The culture practices in this course are recommendations, not part of the policy.

sources.title: ADA.gov, ADA Requirements: Effective Communication
sources.note: Federal guidance on auxiliary aids and services, primary consideration to the person's choice, and undue burden for state and local governments. It addresses communication with the public; employee accommodation follows the employment provisions and state policy.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services, Content and writing guidelines
sources.note: DHS guidance on plain language for public content, including writing for first-read understanding and a fifth- to sixth-grade target when the subject allows. It does not cover alternative formats such as Braille or audio.
